item.title: WAV looper
item.description: To gain hands-on experience of working with cross-task data streams in an RTOS environment, audio playback from an SD card is a good place…
item.content:encoded:
To gain hands-on experience of working with cross-task data streams in an RTOS environment, audio playback from an SD card is a good place to start. You can hear immediately when there is an issue with the handling of the stream.

The aim was to make a prototype device with a touch screen user interface to control the behaviour of the device, an SD card to read WAV file audio data from, and an I2S interface to send audio data out of.

Watch the Video

WAV files

WAV files are ideal for an embedded environment, as the file format contains uncompressed pulse-code modulation data, which can directly be sent to an audio chip. This means there is no overhead for decompression and decoding. The header of the WAV file contains all the relevant data needed to process the data.

  • Sample rate
  • Number of audio channels
  • Bits per sample
  • Audio format
  • Location and size of the audio data

Rendering the WAV file

A selected region of the WAV file was rendered in the UI. This was done by using the header data of the audio file to calculate the bars that needed to be rendered to represent a section of the audio file.

RTOS

The system was made up of 3 main tasks:

  • SD card task reading data from the SPI interface connected to the SD card.
  • I2S audio task sending audio data out to an audio chip.
  • UI task with an SPI connection to a display and an SPI connection to a touch screen controller.

The basic flow of audio data is from the SD card into audio buffers. The audio buffers are then handed off to the audio task via queue messages, and the audio buffer data is sent out via I2S.

The SD card and I2S interface don't necessarily operate at the same rate, and so a reasonable buffer size is needed to enable the producer and consumer tasks to work together. If I2S drains the audio buffer data faster than the SD task can provide new audio data, then the audio stream will be interrupted and the result will be audible.

Audio Buffers

Two audio buffers were created. The SD card producer task filled one buffer, then used a queue message to hand off ownership of the buffer to the audio I2S task. The SD card task then started filling the second buffer. When the I2S audio task was finished with the first buffer, ownership of the two buffers was swapped via queue message signalling. This then continued.

An alternative method would be to have a shared ring buffer, and then use queue messages to signal the head and tail positions in the ring buffer once a batch of processing has completed.

item.title: Virtual Terminal Client
item.description: The ISOBUS standard allows for the creation of custom control systems. As a demonstration, a Virtual Terminal (VT) is used with a VT client…
item.content:encoded:
The ISOBUS standard allows for the creation of custom control systems. As a demonstration, a Virtual Terminal (VT) is used with a VT client connected to a pump and a flow meter to create a minimal watering system.

Watch the Video

VT Client

To interact with an ISOBUS Virtual Terminal (VT), a VT client must perform the following steps as defined by the standard:

  1. Undergo CAN bus address claiming.
  2. Listen for the VT status message.
  3. Send the Working Set Master message.
  4. Begin transmitting VT client status messages.
  5. Upload its serialised user interface using the transport protocol for packetisation.
  6. Send user interface updates and listen for user interface events.

I used Pool Edit to create a minimal ISOBUS user interface consisting of a bar graph and two buttons.

The VT client hardware is connected to a pump through a PWM driver and to a flow meter connected to an input pin configured with an interrupt to monitor pulse counts.

Once the VT client is initialised, the calculated and scaled flow rate value is sent to the VT to update the bar graph on the user interface using an object ID reference.

When a button is pressed on the VT, a message is sent to the VT client containing an object ID reference and a key code value. The VT client then performs the action associated with that object ID and key code. In this demonstration, the action adjusts the PWM output, which controls the pump speed.

item.title: LoRaWAN Network
item.description: To get familiar with the inner workings of a LoRaWAN network, I set up a network using a single basic LoRa node, a Heltec HT-M00 Gateway…
item.content:encoded:
To get familiar with the inner workings of a LoRaWAN network, I set up a network using a single basic LoRa node, a Heltec HT-M00 Gateway, and a ChirpStack server.

Watch the Video

LoRaWAN Node

A node will have a base frequency, which is determined by legal regulations in your jurisdiction, and will dictate the physical antenna used. Radio channels are then created by dividing sections of frequency bands based on the selected bandwidth, derived from the base frequency.

LoRa module settings for a LoRaWAN network:

Setting Value
Spreading Factor SF7–SF12
Bandwidth 125 kHz
Coding Rate 4/5
CRC Enabled
Sync Word 0x34
Preamble 8
  • The coding rate is the proportion of useful data to error correction data.
  • The spreading factor defines the time-on-air for each transmission (higher SF = longer range but slower data rate).
  • The sync word is used to isolate LoRaWAN network traffic from other LoRa networks.

The Device ID used by the node is in little-endian format.

Frequency channel usage is defined by regional legislation. In short, specific frequency channels should not be overused.

Specifications are provided by the LoRa Alliance:

https://resources.lora-alliance.org/

LoRaWAN Gateway

The gateway listens on multiple frequencies, receives and demodulates LoRaWAN radio packets, and then passes the data to the application layer.

The LoRa node and gateway must have frequency settings that correspond to each other.

The Heltec HT-M00 Gateway uses the Semtech UDP packet forwarder protocol to forward data received from a LoRaWAN node to the network server.

LoRaWAN Network Server

The network server handles session establishment, payload decryption, and network routing.

Activation By Personalization (ABP)

If a LoRaWAN node uses ABP to connect to a network server, it can start sending data immediately. There is no need for a join procedure to establish a session.

The LoRaWAN network server must know a node’s:

  • Device Address (4-byte little-endian identifier)
  • Network Session Key (NwkSKey)
  • Application Session Key (AppSKey)

Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) is used to encrypt data and ensure authenticity.
